specPoints.text: understand acids and bases in terms of proton transfer
understand that an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor

primer.text: From Acids, Alkalis & Titrations you know acids as sources of hydrogen ions and alkalis as sources of hydroxide ions. This note deepens both definitions with proton transfer: an acid hands a proton over, and a base takes it in. The same two examples, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, show each role in action.

lessons.title: Proton transfer and acids
lessons.opening: The earlier definitions of acids and bases extend once protons are introduced. An acid is a proton donor: when it dissolves, its molecules ionise and release hydrogen ions, which are simply protons, into the solution. Hydrochloric acid shows this cleanly, splitting into H+ and Cl- ions in water.
keyPoints: An acid is a proton donor.
Acids ionise in solution, releasing hydrogen ions, which are protons.
The H+ ions released make the aqueous solution acidic.
Hydrochloric acid ionises to give H+ and Cl- ions in water.
A proton and a hydrogen ion are two names for the same particle.

low.restatement: An acid hands out protons, and a hydrogen ion is a proton, so saying an acid releases H+ ions says exactly the same thing in different words. Every acid in water ionises the same way, which is why acidic solutions all share the same core chemistry no matter which acid was dissolved.
low.analogy: An acid is a generous friend handing out identical sweets, the protons, to anyone who will take them, and every taster reacts the same way to the same sweet.
low.examPointer: Use the words donor and proton explicitly; naming H+ as the proton earns the chemistry link and one easy mark.

medium.restatement: The proton-transfer definition explains why acids behave as they do in water: their molecules ionise, releasing hydrogen ions, and a hydrogen ion is exactly a proton. Hydrochloric acid provides the standard example, splitting into H+ and Cl- so that the acidic properties of the solution come from the donated protons now free in it.
medium.analogy: Picture a postman delivering identical letters to every house on the street: the acid delivers identical protons to the water, and every house reacts the same way.
medium.examPointer: Link the three ideas in one line: proton donor, hydrogen ion, and the acidity of the resulting solution.

check.stem: In proton-transfer language, what is an acid?

options.explanation: Donating protons is the defining behaviour of an acid in this language.
Accepting protons is the base's role; the acid gives them away.
Electron donation describes metals in redox; acids deal in protons.
Neutrons play no part in acid-base chemistry.

check.stem: What particle is released when an acid ionises in water?

options.text: The hydrogen ion, H+, which is a proton
options.explanation: Ionising releases H+ ions, and each one is exactly a proton.
Hydroxide ions come from bases, never from acids.
Electrons are not released into solution by acids; protons are.

options.text: Nothing is released; the acid stays whole
options.explanation: Ionising means splitting apart, which is how the protons end up free.

check.stem: Into which ions does hydrochloric acid split in water?

options.explanation: The note's example equation shows hydrochloric acid giving one hydrogen ion and one chloride ion.
Those are the ions of sodium hydroxide, the base example.
The charges are reversed; hydrogen carries the positive charge here.
Those are gases, not the ions formed when the acid dissolves.

check.stem: Why do all acidic solutions show similar reactions?

options.text: They all contain the same reactive particle, the hydrogen ion
options.explanation: Because every acid releases H+, the chemistry of the solution is the chemistry of that one ion.
Only hydrochloric acid makes chloride ions; other acids release different partners.

options.text: They all have the same colour
options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant; the shared particle explains the shared behaviour.

options.text: They all come from the same laboratory bottle
options.explanation: Origin is irrelevant; the shared hydrogen ion is the reason.

check.stem: Which phrase correctly completes: the acidity of a solution is caused by?

options.text: The H+ ions released by the acid
options.explanation: The presence of hydrogen ions is precisely what makes the solution acidic.

options.text: The OH- ions released by the acid
options.explanation: Acids release H+; OH- would make the solution alkaline.
Pure water is neutral; the acid's protons create the acidity.

options.text: The stirring that dissolves the acid
options.explanation: Stirring only speeds dissolving; the ions cause the acidity.

lessons.title: Bases (Alkalis)
lessons.opening: Bases, often called alkalis when dissolved, take the opposite role: they are proton acceptors. In water they release hydroxide ions, OH-, and these ions are what accept the protons, which is also what makes the solution alkaline. Sodium hydroxide is the standard example, coming apart into Na+ and OH- ions.
keyPoints: They release OH- ions in solution, and these accept the protons.
The hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline.
Sodium hydroxide splits into Na+ and OH- ions in water.
Acid and base are mirror roles: one gives a proton, the other takes it.

low.restatement: A base takes protons in, using its hydroxide ions, which is why alkaline solutions pair so neatly with acidic ones. Sodium hydroxide dissolving into Na+ and OH- shows the acceptor ready for action.
low.analogy: If the acid is the friend handing out sweets, the base is the friend with an empty bag, collecting every sweet offered.
low.examPointer: Keep the pairing visible in answers: donor with acid, acceptor with base, and OH- as the collecting ion.

medium.restatement: The base completes the transfer: dissolved bases release hydroxide ions, and the hydroxide is the species that actually accepts each proton, which is why the solution turns alkaline. Sodium hydroxide illustrates the family, separating into Na+ and OH- so that every acidic proton arriving has an acceptor waiting for it.
medium.analogy: Think of a cloakroom: the acid hands coats over, the hydroxide ions run the counter taking them in, and the transaction only completes when both are present.
medium.examPointer: Explain questions may ask why alkalis neutralise acids; the answer is proton transfer from donor to acceptor, making water.

check.stem: In proton-transfer language, what is a base?

options.explanation: Taking protons in is the defining behaviour of a base.
Donating is the acid's role; the base receives.
Electron transfer belongs to redox chemistry, not acid-base work.

options.text: A substance that makes no ions
options.explanation: Dissolved bases do ionise, releasing the hydroxide ions that accept protons.

check.stem: Which ion actually accepts the proton when an acid meets an alkali?

options.explanation: The base releases OH- ions precisely so that they can accept the incoming protons.
Na+ is a spectator here; the hydroxide does the accepting.
Chloride belongs to the acid's side and takes no part in accepting the proton.
Water is formed by the transfer; the hydroxide ion is the acceptor that makes it.

check.stem: Into which ions does sodium hydroxide split when it dissolves?

options.explanation: The note's example shows sodium hydroxide giving one sodium ion and one hydroxide ion.
Those are hydrochloric acid's ions.
The charges are reversed; sodium is positive and hydroxide negative.
That split is not how the hydroxide ion comes apart; it stays whole as OH-.

check.stem: Why is a dissolved base often called an alkali?

options.text: Because its released hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline
options.explanation: The OH- ions the base releases are what give the solution its alkaline character.
Taste is never the criterion; the released ions are.

options.text: Because it only dissolves in acid
options.explanation: Bases dissolve in water, not specifically in acid.

options.text: Because it donates protons like an acid
options.explanation: That would make it an acid; bases accept instead.

check.stem: Hydrochloric acid meets sodium hydroxide in solution. Which pairing describes the transfer?

options.text: HCl donates a proton and the OH- ion accepts it
options.explanation: The acid's H+ hands over to the base's hydroxide, and water is the result.

options.text: NaOH donates a proton and Cl- accepts it
options.explanation: Sodium hydroxide has no proton to donate; hydroxide accepts protons.

options.text: Na+ donates a proton to H+
options.explanation: Na+ carries no proton to give; it watches the transfer happen.

options.text: Cl- donates a proton to OH-
options.explanation: Cl- is not a proton carrier; the donor is the acid's H+.

glossary.definition: The positive particle that a hydrogen ion is; what acids donate and bases accept.
A proton donor, which ionises in water releasing hydrogen ions.
A proton acceptor, which in water releases hydroxide ions able to take protons in.
A dissolved base whose hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline.
The role of handing a particle over, taken by the acid for protons.
The role of receiving a particle, taken by the base for protons.

workedExample.prompt: a) Define an acid and a base in terms of proton transfer. b) Show, with equations, how hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide ionise in water. c) When the two solutions are mixed, which ion accepts the proton and what product forms?
steps: a) An acid is a proton donor; a base is a proton acceptor.
b) HCl (aq) → H+ (aq) + Cl- (aq): the acid ionises, releasing protons into the solution. NaOH (s) → Na+ (aq) + OH- (aq): the base releases hydroxide ions.
c) The hydroxide ion, OH-, accepts the proton, and the product is water: H+ + OH- → H2O.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. b) HCl → H+ + Cl-; NaOH → Na+ + OH-. c) OH- accepts the proton, forming water.
